name: Magnoliaceae

lineage_context.teaching_goal: Teach Magnolia grandiflora through annular stipule scars, very large terminal flowers with numerous spirally arranged tepals/stamens/pistils, and a cone-like aggregate of follicles releasing red arillate seeds.

project_scope.note: Magnolia grandiflora is accepted by current Kew and its native range extends to Texas. Exact target-zone nativity remains species-level work.

family_diagnostics.where_to_look_first: Inspect a twig node and then a flower. Magnoliaceae leaves have stipules that surround the stem/bud and leave a conspicuous annular scar; flowers are large and terminal with many tepals, stamens and pistils.
family_diagnostics.vegetative: Aromatic trees or shrubs; leaves alternate, simple, entire. Stipules are characteristic and usually leave a ring scar around the twig node.
family_diagnostics.reproductive: Flowers solitary, terminal, typically large. Tepals 6–18 or more in whorls of 3; stamens numerous, free and spirally arranged; pistils numerous and superior on an elongated receptacle.
family_diagnostics.fruit: Cone-like aggregate of many follicles in Magnolia. Each follicle can release 1–2 seeds with a red/pink/orange oily aril, often hanging briefly by a funiculus.
family_diagnostics.field_tip: Annular stipule scar + huge many-parted terminal flower + cone-like aggregate fruit = Magnoliaceae/Magnolia.

visual_lesson.teaching_order: stipule scar → giant terminal flower → spiral stamens/pistils → elongate receptacle → follicetum → red arillate seed → Lauraceae contrast
visual_lesson.intro: Magnolia shows the 'many repeated parts' floral architecture especially clearly: instead of a tiny 3-part laurel flower, one flower carries numerous tepals, stamens and pistils on an elongated axis.

steps.title: 1 · Find the ring around the twig
steps.look_for: A complete annular scar encircling the twig where a stipule once wrapped the bud/stem.
steps.why_it_matters: This is a high-value vegetative Magnoliaceae clue and a clean contrast with exstipulate Lauraceae.

steps.title: 2 · Count beyond five
steps.look_for: Many tepals rather than a fixed 4- or 5-part flower, plus numerous stamens surrounding the central gynoecium.
steps.why_it_matters: Introduces the repeated-part magnoliid flower plan.

steps.title: 3 · Trace the spiral reproductive axis
steps.look_for: Stamens and many pistils arranged spirally on an elongated receptacle.
steps.why_it_matters: Explains how the flower later becomes a cone-like aggregate fruit.

steps.title: 4 · Follow the gynoecium into a follicetum
steps.look_for: Numerous woody follicles coalesced around an elongate axis, producing the familiar cone-like magnolia fruit.
steps.why_it_matters: Connects many pistils in the flower to many fruit units.

steps.title: 5 · Find the red arillate seed
steps.look_for: Red or orange seed emerging from a follicle and sometimes hanging by a threadlike funiculus.
steps.why_it_matters: A very memorable late-season family cue.

steps.title: 6 · Southern magnolia door
steps.look_for: Evergreen tree; thick glossy leaves, often rusty/red-brown felted beneath; huge fragrant white flowers.
steps.why_it_matters: Distinguishes the sole project magnolia concept quickly.

comparisons.title: Magnoliaceae vs Lauraceae
comparisons.rule: Magnoliaceae has stipules/node rings, very large terminal flowers, numerous stamens/pistils, and aggregate fruits. Lauraceae lacks stipules, has tiny trimerous flowers with valvate anthers, and usually a single-seeded fleshy fruit.

comparisons.title: Magnoliaceae vs Saururaceae
comparisons.rule: Magnoliaceae is woody with a conspicuous perianth and many floral organs; Saururaceae is a wetland herb whose tiny flowers lack a perianth entirely and are packed into a raceme/spike.

visual_lesson.caveat: Large white flowers alone are not enough. The annular stipule scar, many free stamens/pistils, and aggregate follicle fruit are the transferable family characters.

genera.fast_cue: annular stipule scar + giant terminal many-parted flower + cone-like follicetum + red arillate seed

taxonomy_reconciliation.note: Accepted by current Kew; native range is southeastern U.S.A. to Texas.
